1.pericope_label: Except the Lord build the house: labour, watching and anxious bread set against a blessing given in sleep

schools.summary: Augustine treats the name in the title as a moral difficulty, holding that the good delivered through a man who fell is to be attributed to God and the sin to the man, and citing the fall of the first man and of an angel.

Calvin defends the ascription against the Jewish reading of the prefixed letter, widens house and city into the family and the commonwealth, and guards the saying from any disparagement of labour, since God did not mean us to be blocks of wood; Gill instances the builders of Babel.

Henry makes the psalm a father instruction to a son apt to lean on his own forecast, warns that God does not build where foundations are laid in oppression, and rebukes those who rob their sleep to pay their cares; Spurgeon instances Babel and the ruin of ambitious builders.

Clarke reviews the versions on the title and dates the psalm to the second temple under Nehemiah, derives son, daughter and house from one root meaning to build, and reads the sleep off the watches of the rebuilding; Wesley takes the gift as given freely without immoderate toil.

Ellicott insists the house is any house and not the temple, and sets out both renderings of the closing clause with proverbs and poetry on either side; Keil and Delitzsch explain the title from two allusions and from the proverb-song form, and report an early expositor who preferred the days of Zerubbabel.

debates: Who wrote the psalm, and when? Calvin defends Solomon and rejects as absurd the Jewish reading that makes the prefixed letter mean for rather than of, since such a title always designates the author; Keil and Delitzsch think the name added only because of two allusions and the proverb-song form, and report an early expositor who found the psalm better suited to the rebuilding under Zerubbabel; Clarke reviews the versions and judges it composed for the second temple under Nehemiah by some prophet; Henry keeps the name but makes the psalm a father instruction to that son; Augustine leaves the historical question and treats the fall of the named man as the real difficulty.

Does God give sleep, or give while his beloved sleep? Ellicott sets out both renderings, notes that the old versions make sleep the direct object and so the gift itself, and holds that the adverbial sense suits the context beyond question, supporting it with a Greek and a German proverb while granting that old association pleads beautifully for the other; Wesley takes the adverbial sense as a gift given without immoderate toil; Clarke reads it off the rota of watches at the rebuilding, by which the workers got their rest.
outliers: Augustine argues that the good delivered through a man who afterwards fell must be attributed to God and the sin to the man, since the first man fell in Paradise and an angel fell from heaven, so that no hope is to be placed in any among men.

Clarke derives the Hebrew words for son, daughter and house from one root meaning to build, on the ground that sons and daughters constitute a family as truly as stones and timber constitute a building.
themes: human effort dependent on a blessing
the family and the city under one rule

3.pericope_label: Lo, children are an heritage of the Lord: the arrows, the full quiver, and the enemies in the gate

schools.summary: Gill limits the blessing to good children, takes the quiver of the house full of them, and reports the versions that render the clause of a desire filled rather than a quiver.

Clarke contrasts the portions of the childless rich and the fruitful poor, explains the children of the youth by physiology and then disclaims physiological exegesis, applies the quiver to the wife rather than the house, and reads the gate of marauders rather than of courts; Wesley explains the children of the youth domestically and takes the gate wholly of courts of judicature.

Ellicott makes the heritage a heritage from God, glosses the children of the youth as the offspring of an early marriage, and prefers a martial sense in the last clause while granting the forensic; Keil and Delitzsch distinguish an inheritance given at the free will of the giver from one held by right, and a recompense of free judgment from a payment owed.

debates: What is the quiver that is full? Gill takes it of the house full of children and notes the versions that render the clause of a desire filled instead; Clarke submits that the metaphor is more congenial if the quiver is the wife, so that the blessing is a fruitful wife rather than a full house, and defends the figure as Jewish in style and paralleled in a later book.

Is the closing clause martial or forensic? Ellicott argues that after the warrior and his arrows a martial image is to be expected, so that the parents are not discomfited but challenge their enemies in the gates, while granting that the gate is commonly the place of judgment; Wesley takes it wholly of courts of judicature and of a cause pleaded without fear; Clarke weighs both, allowing that a man falsely accused has as many witnesses as children, and declares for the house defended against marauders.
outliers: Clarke supplies a physiological account of why the children of youth are stronger than those of age, and then draws back to say that the interpretation of Scripture will seldom admit of physiological details.

Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the terms carefully, holding that the inheritance here is not one held by hereditary right but one given at the free will of the giver, and the reward not a payment made in duty bound but a recompense looked for according to promise yet never to be demanded.
themes: strength in the offspring of early marriage
a household defended by its own sons
